title: Integrated multiclass driver ctDNA profiling enables MPNST detection and monitoring in NF1 patients.
abstract: We developed and internally cross-validated an integrated circulating tumor DNA assay incorporating single nucleotide variants (SNVs), insertions/deletions (indels), copy number alterations (CNAs), and structural variants (SVs) to distinguish neurofibromatosis type 1 patients with malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors (MPNST) from those with benign plexiform neurofibromas and tumor-free controls. Among 82 participants, the assay achieved an AUC of 0.917 versus 0.737 for off-target genome-wide CNA analysis. We detected disease-specific alterations, relapse eighty days before diagnosis, and molecular clearance consistent with remission.
authors: Paul A Jones; Aaron U Bektas; Jeffrey J Szymanski; R Taylor Sundby; John S A Chrisinger; Peter K Harris; Mark I Zoberi; Kara Weekley; Sanita Burgic; Stacey Chamberlain; Faridi Qaium; Jack F Shern; Aadel A Chaudhuri; Angela C Hirbe
methods: Methods Study design and patient enrollment Biospecimens were prospectively collected between 2020 and 2024 at Washington University in St. Louis (WUSTL) under protocols approved by the Institutional Review Board (IRB 201903142, 201203042). Eligible participants included individuals with confirmed clinical or radiographic diagnosis of plexiform neurofibromas (PN) by NF1-expert clinicians and those with biopsy-proven malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors (MPNST). NF1 diagnoses were established using NIH consensus criteria. Pathological confirmation of MPNST diagnosis was conducted by board-certified sarcoma pathologists. A total of 44 patients with PN and 26 patients with MPNST were enrolled. From the MPNST cohort, 45 serial plasma samples were collected across multiple timepoints to evaluate tumor dynamics. No PN participant developed clinically diagnosed MPNST or became deceased during follow-up, with median (mean) post-baseline imaging follow-up of 896 days (974 days), clinical follow-up of 1088 days (1135 days), and longitudinal follow-up confirming survival of 1219 days (1237 days). PN patients with symptoms concerning for malignant transformation were excluded. An additional group of 12 healthy participants (with an additional 12 for PACT artifact background polishing) provided blood samples for background modeling. All participants provided written informed consent prior to enrollment. Samples included and excluded in the study are detailed in Fig.  S3 . Longitudinal clinical timelines for participants with serial plasma sampling were reconstructed by manual abstraction from EHR source documentation and are shown in Fig.  S4.  For each participant, plasma draw dates were aligned to contemporaneous clinical surveillance events, including radiology report impressions for imaging assessments, operative reports and pathology reports for surgical procedures and margin status, and pathology reports for biopsies. Imaging categories in Fig.  S4  are taken directly from the corresponding radiology report impression at that timepoint, with NED timepoints reflecting no definitive radiographic malignancy while allowing for report-described indeterminate or suspicious findings. Disease-bearing timepoints were identified based on EHR clinical documentation of active MPNST, supported by biopsy or resection pathology when available. Surgical events and resection margin status were similarly abstracted from operative and pathology documentation. Figure  S4  is provided to transparently display the complete serial record underlying the longitudinal trajectories and is not intended for formal comparative inference across event types or timepoints. For the primary classifier analysis and ROC and AUC evaluation, we included all disease-bearing MPNST plasma draws and all non-malignant comparator samples (PN baseline and healthy controls), excluding the panel-of-normals samples. Clinically disease-free surveillance draws (NED timepoints) from MPNST participants were analyzed only for longitudinal display and draw-level calling, and were not used for model training, tuning, or ROC and AUC evaluation. Sample collection and processing Peripheral venous blood (10 to 30 mL total) was collected in three 10 mL K2EDTA tubes (BD Biosciences) and stored at 4 °C until processing within 4 h of phlebotomy. Blood samples underwent initial centrifugation at 1200 ×  g  for 10 min at ambient temperature to separate plasma from cellular components. The plasma supernatant was carefully transferred into DNA low-bind microcentrifuge tubes and subjected to a secondary centrifugation at 1800 ×  g  for 5 min to further deplete cellular debris. Clarified plasma was aliquoted into 1.5 mL microcentrifuge tubes and stored at −80°C until DNA extraction. The residual cellular fraction (plasma-depleted whole blood, PDWB) was also aliquoted and stored at −80 °C for germline DNA isolation. Plasma was visually inspected immediately after processing and again at thaw. Plasma samples were excluded for hemolysis if plasma was visibly red or pink, with a distinct red tint compared with normal straw-colored plasma. Tumor tissue was obtained at the time of clinical biopsy or surgery, following institutional pathology workflows. FFPE blocks or snap-frozen specimens were retained for molecular studies if excess diagnostic tissue was available. MPNST and PN samples were sequenced within the same Illumina flow cell lanes to mitigate batch effects. cfDNA and genomic DNA extraction Circulating cell-free DNA (cfDNA) was isolated from 2 to 8 mL of thawed plasma using the Qiagen Circulating Nucleic Acid Kit in conjunction with the QIAvac vacuum manifold system, following manufacturer protocols. Germline DNA was extracted from PDWB using the Qiagen DNeasy Blood and Tissue Kit. Tumor DNA was isolated using either the AllPrep DNA/RNA FFPE Kit for FFPE sections or the DNeasy kit for frozen tissue specimens. Extracted DNA was quantified using the Qubit dsDNA High Sensitivity Assay (Thermo Fisher Scientific), and fragment size distributions were assessed using the Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer. For plasma cfDNA specimens, sample level blood volume collected, plasma volume processed, and plasma cfDNA yield normalized to plasma volume (ng/mL plasma) are reported in Data S3. Plasma-derived samples were excluded if they were primarily composed of high-molecular-weight DNA, defined as more than 75 percent of total DNA signal outside the cfDNA size range of 70 to 450 bp. Samples with insufficient cfDNA yield for library preparation were excluded from downstream analysis, defined as total extracted cfDNA yield below 10 ng. To optimize downstream library preparation and hybridization, tumor and germline DNA were fragmented to a modal size of approximately 200 base pairs using a Covaris LE220 focused ultrasonicator. cfDNA underwent no additional shearing. Targeted panel design and in silico validation A custom hybrid capture panel was developed using the Roche HyperDesign platform to target refined genomic regions totaling ~304 kb. Regions were consolidated from an initial 3615 candidates to reduce redundancy and improve coverage efficiency. Genes were organized into three tiers. Tier 1 included genes with high recurrence, whole-gene coverage, and relevance to early malignant transformation, particularly  CDKN2A ,  CDKN2B ,  TP53 ,  SUZ12 , and  EED . These regions were selected to support detection of inactivating SNVs, splice-altering variants, and structural variants such as inversions or deletions. Tier 2 included candidate oncogenes located on chromosome 8q and associated with tumorigenesis upon amplification. Tier 3 comprised a mixture of lower-prevalence genes,  NF1 , and genes associated with clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential. Probe selection aimed to maximize specificity and minimize off-target binding. In silico benchmarking was performed using publicly available cancer datasets and the Genomics of MPNST (GeM) cohort. Library preparation and sequencing Library construction was performed using the KAPA HyperPrep Kit (Kapa Biosystems, catalog no. KK8502). cfDNA libraries were prepared from 32 ng of input DNA whenever possible; for samples yielding <32 ng, a minimum of 10 ng of DNA was used for preparation. Libraries underwent 12 cycles of pre-capture PCR, with a subset undergoing up to 15 cycles due to low DNA mass or low post-PCR yield. Tumor and germline libraries were constructed from a similar 32 ng of input DNA. Fragment size was confirmed with the Agilent Bioanalyzer. A total of 1.5 µg of pooled library DNA (12-plex) was used for hybridization capture with the custom panel. Libraries were pooled with equivalent mass input across samples. Following capture, libraries underwent 17 cycles of post-enrichment PCR amplification. Sequencing was performed on an Illumina HiSeq 4000 system (Illumina Inc., San Diego, CA) with 2 × 150 bp paired-end reads and an 8-base indexing read. Mean unique sequencing depth was approximately on-target 1032x, 674x, and 300x for cfDNA, germline and tumor, respectively. All SNV, small indel, CNA, and SV calling was performed using the Pipeline for the Analysis of ctDNA (PACT), developed at Washington University School of Medicine (Webster et al., Bioinformatics 2023). PACT is a unified workflow designed to reproducibly identify single-nucleotide variants, indels, copy number alterations, and structural variants from ctDNA sequencing data. The pipeline integrates multiple variant calling strategies with support for matched controls and unmatched healthy plasma background models to reduce artifacts and increase specificity, particularly for low-frequency ctDNA events. It is distributed as a Common Workflow Language (CWL) implementation and is freely available at  https://github.com/ChrisMaherLab/PACT . For this project, paired-end reads were demultiplexed using sample-specific index barcodes and aligned to the hg19 reference genome using BWA MEM v0.7.17 with default parameters. Adapter and quality trimming were not performed as a separate FASTQ preprocessing step prior to alignment. Overlapping mate pairs were not merged and were handled as standard paired-end alignments. Alignments were converted to BAM, sorted, and indexed using SAMtools v1.13–1.22. PCR duplicates were identified and removed or marked using either SAMtools markdup or Picard v2.18 as appropriate for downstream CNA, SV, SNV, and indel analyses. Quality control metrics were collected using SAMtools flagstat, FastQC, and BEDTools coverageBed. Only properly paired reads with a mapping quality ≥30 were retained for downstream analysis. For libraries, consensus deduplication was performed prior to variant calling, and all reported depth metrics and all allele fraction and read support thresholds were computed on consensus, deduplicated reads representing unique molecules. SNV and indel detection SNV and small indel detection was performed using the Pipeline for the Analysis of ctDNA (PACT), which integrates an ensemble of Mutect, Strelka, VarScan, and Pindel under relaxed, sensitivity-optimized parameters. Variant calls were normalized using Vt and annotated with VEP. Standardized read counts were computed using bam-readcount, and additional filters were applied based on read depth, mapping quality, allele fraction (AF), population frequency (gnomAD), and signal observed in background controls. To mitigate low-VAF artifacts, variant evidence was restricted to high-quality bases, and bases with Phred quality <30 were not used for SNV and indel support. In addition, caller-provided read position and read-end annotations were retained within PACT, and variants with support concentrated at read ends or soft-clipped positions were flagged and filtered. Background artifact suppression was implemented by genotyping a preconfigured panel of 12 healthy plasma samples with GATK HaplotypeCaller and removing variants observed in >10% of controls. Variants detected in germline from unrelated individuals were also systematically excluded when consistent with PCR slippage or mismapping artifacts within the same sequencing lane. Final variant calls were assigned confidence rankings based on caller agreement, read support, AF, and filter annotations. Consequence categories were defined for visualization and classification. Splice variants were grouped as Donor, Acceptor, Region, or Other. Missense variants were annotated using PolyPhen 2 and SIFT. PolyPhen 2 and SIFT outputs were used to assign missense variants into intermediate impact groups, protein disrupting when PolyPhen 2 supported a damaging interpretation and SIFT supported a deleterious interpretation, likely not disrupting when both supported a benign or tolerated interpretation, and variants of unknown significance (VUS) for intermediate or discordant calls. These intermediate groups were used for reporting and visualization and were subsequently mapped into the unified per-gene ordinal severity encoding used by the classifier to harmonize missense with splice-altering and truncating events. Truncating loss-of-function (LoF) variants included frameshift, stop-gained, and start-lost events. Diagnostic group, gene identity, and variant confidence were used to control inclusion for downstream analysis. Within PACT, stringent quantitative thresholds were applied. For cfDNA samples, variants were retained only if they passed all internal PACT filters and had AF > 0.0005 with alternate allele depth ≥8. Tumor variants were included if AF exceeded 0.05 with alternate allele depth ≥8, and were excluded if flagged for contamination, germline origin, or normal artifact. All allele fraction and depth thresholds were applied on unique, deduplicated read evidence, and sensitivity for very low allele fraction events is therefore constrained by the achieved locus level depth after filtering. Across 101 non-panel-of-normals cfDNA plasma samples, 17 samples had zero passing variants and among 2,195 passing variants (including noncoding), variant-level VAFs had a mean of 1.05%, a median of 0.304%, and an IQR of 0.186% to 0.514%. Noncoding variants were not removed but tracked separately for annotation and visualization. Copy number alteration detection Copy number alterations were detected using CNVkit v0.9.6 within the PACT workflow. Bin-level log₂ coverage ratios were calculated between cfDNA samples and controls, then corrected for GC content and repeat bias. Ratios were aggregated to gene-level log₂ values using a trimmed average to reduce the influence of outlier bins. Regions with low plasma read depth or excessive variability were excluded. Gene-level values were normalized using a background reference of expected copy-neutral regions and off-target bins to correct for global technical variation. Per-gene standard deviations were estimated from healthy controls and used to calculate z-scores per sample.  ATRX  (due to X-chromosome effects) and known artifact-prone loci were excluded. CNA log₂ values and z-scores for  TP53 ,  CDKN2A/B ,  SUZ12 ,  EED , and chromosome 8q (averaged across candidate oncogenes) were retained as input features for the integrated classification model. These processed values were also used in violin plots and individual gene-level bar plots. Structural variant analysis Structural variants were identified using an ensemble approach with Delly, Lumpy, and Manta run in sensitive modes to generate an inclusive candidate set. Delly calls were generated with delly calls and were not subjected to the default delly filter step. Lumpy calls were generated using lumpyexpress with the minimum weight lowered to 3 (-m 3). Manta was run with default settings, but only the candidate SV output was used for downstream processing rather than relying on Manta’s final filtered SV outputs. SV candidates were merged with SURVIVOR to define consensus events using a maximum breakpoint distance of 100 bp and a minimum SV size of 200 bp, with same strand not required and SV distance not estimated. Consensus SVs were retained only if supported by at least two callers. Consensus calls were then filtered to retain events originating from targeted panel regions, including a ± 200 bp breakpoint wingspan, and to remove alignment prone artifacts by excluding SVs with any breakpoint in blacklisted regions and excluding SVs with more than one breakpoint in low complexity regions. To suppress germline events and systematic false positives in cfDNA, consensus SVs were aggregated across the cohort and re-genotyped using SVTyper across all samples, matched controls, and a panel of healthy plasma sequenced with the same panel. Any SV with evidence in any control or healthy plasma was excluded. For cfDNA, retained SVs were additionally required to have both split read and discordant paired end read support, with at least two total supporting reads. Tumor SVs were evaluated using the same multi caller requirement but without the cfDNA read evidence threshold. Surviving calls were annotated with SnpEff and reported in BEDPE format, including caller support and read evidence summaries. No whitelist was applied. For integrated analysis, we further restricted to high confidence SVs affecting  TP53 ,  SUZ12 , or  EED , and duplications involving targeted chromosome 8 regions. Tumor–cfDNA concordance analyses Tumor–cfDNA concordance was assessed in matched plasma–tumor pairs using modality-specific metrics designed to be robust to variable ctDNA fraction and clinical sampling constraints. For CNAs, concordance was evaluated using Spearman correlation between tumor and plasma gene-level CNA profiles. Gene-level CNA values were obtained from CNVkit-derived outputs after GC and repeat correction and gene-level aggregation. Pairwise plasma–tumor Spearman correlations were computed across the recurrent CNA gene set used for cohort-level comparisons. Cohort-level CNA concordance was quantified by correlating the mean plasma CNA profile for each clinical group with the mean tumor CNA profile across the same gene set. Negative-control comparisons were computed analogously using Healthy plasma versus tumor and PN plasma versus tumor. Participant-level CNA concordance was summarized using an equal-weight approach. Within each participant, Spearman correlations were computed for available matched plasma–tumor comparisons, then combined within participant on the Fisher  z  scale and back-transformed to a participant-level Spearman  ρ . An overall participant-level concordance estimate was obtained by averaging participant-level Fisher  z  values with equal participant weights and back-transforming. Statistical significance for cohort-level Spearman correlations used standard two-sided correlation testing. Statistical significance for the participant-level aggregate concordance used two-sided testing on Fisher  z -transformed participant-level correlations. For SNVs and short indels, concordance was assessed as tumor recovery of plasma sites. A plasma SNV site was counted as recovered if the same genomic position was present in the matched tumor callset under an unfiltered tumor reference, defined as tumor calls after matched-germline subtraction and basic quality processing but prior to applying the more stringent tumor-specific reporting filters used for downstream visualization and feature encoding. The primary summary statistic was the participant-level any-match rate, defined as the fraction of participants with at least one plasma SNV site recovered in the matched tumor. Exact confidence intervals for the any-match rate were computed using binomial methods. Tumor fraction estimation using ichorCNA Tumor fraction was estimated using ichorCNA applied to off-target reads from the targeted hybrid-capture panel, which approximates ultra-low-pass whole genome sequencing. To generate off-target data, we removed reads overlapping the capture target space using bedtools. The target BED was padded by plus or minus 500 bp prior to excision to exclude partial overlaps and edge-adjacent alignments. This identical on-target excision procedure was applied to all cfDNA samples and to the healthy donor samples used to construct the ichorCNA panel of normals. After on-target excision, off-target coverage was summarized genome-wide in large non-overlapping 1 Mb bins across autosomes. Bin-level read counts were GC and mappability corrected using standard ichorCNA resources for 1 Mb binning, and the panel of normals was generated from healthy donor off-target profiles processed identically. ichorCNA was then run to produce a single genome-wide tumor fraction estimate per sample. Bin-wise, chromosome-level, and focal copy-number outputs were not used for downstream analyses, only the genome-wide tumor fraction estimate. Depth summaries are reported in Data S3. cfDNA-based multiclass variant classification model To distinguish malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors (MPNST) from plexiform neurofibromas (PNs) and healthy controls, we developed a logistic regression classifier integrating multiclass genomic features derived from plasma circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA). Feature classes included copy number alterations (CNAs), single nucleotide variants (SNVs), and structural variants (SVs), each processed to preserve biological relevance and maximize classification performance. Model performance was estimated using nested leave-one-out cross-validation, with all preprocessing and feature construction performed within each training fold before scoring the held-out sample. Discrimination metrics included ROC AUC and PR AUC, computed from out-of-fold predictions. Full Cross-Comparison details are in Data S4. Gene-level CNAs were extracted from targeted sequencing data for  CDKN2A/B ,  TP53 ,  SUZ12 ,  EED , and chromosome 8q. For each gene, two metrics were derived: the log₂-transformed depth ratio and a normalized score calculated by dividing the log₂ depth ratio by the standard deviation of that gene’s log₂ depth ratio. All CNA features were scaled within each training fold during cross-validation, and the held-out sample was transformed using parameters that fit in that fold. Eighteen prespecified features were considered for the integrated model and their weights are listed in Data S4, nine of which ultimately had non-zero values. SNVs were assigned functional categories in a defined rank order: loss-of-function, protein-disrupting missense, splice-altering, VUS, non-disrupting missense, synonymous, and other. For each gene, the highest-severity event per sample was retained and encoded on a 0–6 ordinal scale. In addition, a count-based variable was derived for SVs to classify each gene as having a single or multiple variant events. Structural variants were first annotated for predicted functional impact, then encoded for the integrated model based on functional output and relevance to established MPNST drivers, analogous to SNV encoding, and categorized by gene as none, single, or multiple events. Events with known germline presence in unrelated patients were manually excluded to avoid confounding from sequencing artifacts. For ROC and AUC labeling, draws were classified as malignant if collected at an EHR-defined disease-bearing timepoint with active MPNST, supported by pathology when available. Non-malignant samples comprised PN baseline plasma and healthy controls, and NED surveillance draws were excluded from ROC and AUC evaluation.
